in the liver of the dog, unlike in rat, glutamine is the main transporter for nitrogen and carbon from skeletal muscle to liver for synthesis of urea and glucose.

the metabolism of lactate and alanine and glutamin in isolated canine liver cell.
the metabolism of glutamine and its role in the regulation of the metabolism in the fasted and the diabetic dog.
the metabolism of lactate in isolated cells of the liver of the dog.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in the canine liver, glutamine is not only a major transporter of nitrogen from muscle to liver but also a major gluconeogenic precursor.
the dog is a species with high capacity for gluconeogenesis from all three precursors and ureogenesis from lactate and glutamine.
in the fast dog, unlike in fasted rat, alanine is not the main transporter of carbon and nitrogen from muscle to liver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the dog, glutamine is the main transporter to liver of nitrogen for urea synthesis.
in the dog, unlike in rats and man, lactate is a more efficient gluconeogenic precursor in the liver and glutamine a more efficient nitrogenous precursor in the kidney.
lactate and glutamine are the preferred gluconeogenic substrates in the dog, whereas alanine is the preferred substrate for ureogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver cells of dogs and cats have a different metabolism than those of rodents.
the liver is an important organ for the metabolism and regulation of glutamine and glutamine metabolism is a key process in the liver.
the liver of the fasted dog can utilize all of the major substrates that are available in the circulation for gluconeogenesis and ureagenesis.
